questions.prompt: Explain how the budget tracker turns typed amount text into money, and why it does not simply call Number on the input.

keyPoints.text: Number inputs supply text, so the accepted grammar must be defined before converting.
keyPoints.quote: Number inputs supply text. Define its grammar before conversion

keyPoints.text: Number accepts forms that do not belong in a currency workflow.
keyPoints.quote: Number accepts forms that do not belong in this currency workflow.

keyPoints.text: The whole and fractional parts are split, the fraction right-padded, and integer minor units built.
keyPoints.quote: Split whole and fractional text, right-pad the fraction and construct integer minor units.

keyPoints.text: Multiplying arbitrary fractional input does not give an exact result.
keyPoints.quote: Do not multiply arbitrary fractional input and assume an exact result.

keyPoints.text: Totals round each contribution to cents first, which keeps old saved dollars compatible.
keyPoints.quote: Existing saved dollars remain compatible; each total contribution is rounded to cents first.

keyPoints.text: This is not a versioned migration or an arbitrary-precision ledger.
keyPoints.quote: This is not a versioned migration or arbitrary-precision ledger.

questions.prompt: Explain why ordering matters when a change is both kept in memory and written to storage, and what await and try do and do not guarantee.

keyPoints.text: Committing state is its own boundary: serialize the whole candidate, write it, then publish it.
keyPoints.quote: Committing state is a separate boundary: serialize the full candidate, write it, then publish it.

keyPoints.text: If memory changes first and the write fails, the UI shows data that disappears on reload.
keyPoints.quote: If memory changes first and persistence fails, the UI can show data that will disappear after reload.

keyPoints.text: If storage succeeds first and rendering fails, the data is right but the screen is stale.
keyPoints.quote: If persistence succeeds first and rendering fails, the stored data may be correct while the screen is stale.

keyPoints.text: The ordering choice must be deliberate and observable.
keyPoints.quote: the choice must be deliberate and observable

keyPoints.text: await does not make an operation infallible or atomic.
keyPoints.quote: `await` does not make it infallible or atomic

keyPoints.text: Several calls inside one try block are not a database transaction.
keyPoints.quote: calling several functions inside one `try` block does not create a database transaction

keyPoints.text: Atomicity must come from a storage boundary that actually provides it.
keyPoints.quote: Atomicity must come from a storage operation or transaction boundary that actually provides it.

questions.prompt: Explain the zero-amount edit problem: why zero is rejected, what that does to existing records, and how the three positions trade off.

keyPoints.text: A zero-value transaction is a mistake or an empty form, not a fact about finances.
keyPoints.quote: a zero-value income or expense is not a fact about your finances, it is a mistake or an empty form

keyPoints.text: Because edits reuse the same parser, a stored zero record can never be saved again.
keyPoints.quote: **can never be saved again**

keyPoints.text: The record stays readable and deletable, just not editable.
keyPoints.quote: The record is readable and deletable, but not editable.

keyPoints.text: Keeping the rule means one rule, one parser, one place to change it.
keyPoints.quote: One rule, one parser, one place to change it.

keyPoints.text: Allowing zero only on edit makes validity depend on how you reached the form.
keyPoints.quote: Now the validity of a value depends on *how you arrived at the form*

keyPoints.text: Fixing it at the load boundary keeps one input rule and makes the impossible state impossible.
keyPoints.quote: This keeps one rule for input *and* makes the impossible state impossible, which is usually the better trade.

keyPoints.text: Whenever a validator is tightened, ask what it does to existing data.
keyPoints.quote: "what does this rule do to data that already exists?" is a question you must ask every time you tighten a validator
